The Dusky broadbill (Corydon sumatranus) is a striking passerine of the Eurylaimidae family, inhabiting the lowland and submontane forests of Southeast Asia. Eggs of this species, which are incubated at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], require an incubation period of approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] before the nestlings hatch. Upon hatching, the altricial chicks have an initial body mass of 7.6 grams [Ww0 = 7.6 grams], a value derived from measurements of egg dimensions—typically 29.4 millimeters in length and 22.2 millimeters in width—which is consistent with the modest egg size characteristic of this relatively small-bodied bird. The nestling period is brief yet energetically demanding, with chicks growing rapidly under the attentive care of both parents. The development and physiological transitions of the young are closely tied to the thermal environment, as the species is restricted to warm, humid forests where ambient temperatures remain relatively stable throughout the year.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic phase, at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young broadbills achieve their first flight and leave the nest approximately 18 days after hatching [tx = approximately 18 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid fledging period is comparable to that of other tropical passerines and allows the brood to disperse before the onset of heavy monsoon rains. After fledging, the juveniles continue to be fed by the adults for a short period before reaching nutritional independence. The ability to fledge quickly is an adaptation that reduces the window of vulnerability to nest predation, a significant selective pressure in the dense, predator-rich forests this species occupies. The precise timing of fledging is influenced by the local microclimate, but at the core body temperature that facilitates optimal metabolic functioning, this 18-day developmental milestone appears to be consistently observed across its range.

This early pubertal development, expressed in the maturation of gonadal tissues and the onset of reproductive hormone signaling, is an unusual life-history feature for a forest passerine, which often delay maturity for many months. The species appears to channel a substantial portion of its early growth trajectory into rapid reproductive system development, enabling young birds to potentially contribute to the next generation during the same breeding season in which they were born. This strategy may be linked to the relatively high adult mortality rates observed in the wild, favoring early reproduction to offset shorter life expectancies. The timing of this developmental milestone is finely tuned to the species' energetic budget and the consistent food availability of its tropical habitat.

The age at which a Dusky broadbill first successfully breeds, marking its entry into the reproductive population, has been documented at approximately 620.5 days since birth [tR = approximately 620.5 days since birth] when the birds are maintained at their characteristic active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan for the Dusky broadbill in the wild is approximately 11.5 years [am = approximately 11.5 years] when measured under its typical active temperature regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a relatively long duration for a bird of its modest 140 grams [Wwi = 140 grams] asymptotic adult body mass. The species' slow life-history pace—characterized by a delayed first reproduction, modest annual fecundity, and substantial investment in each offspring—aligns it with other tropical forest passerines that have evolved to maximize adult survival in a relatively stable but resource-competitive environment.
